quote: POSIX.1 says that "writes of less than PIPE_BUF bytes must be atomic: the output data is written to the pipe as a contiguous sequence." claim: O_DSYNC guarantees only that write-necessary metadata (e.g. file length) and data reach hardware by the time write() returns (equivalent to fdatasync after each write); O_SYNC additionally flushes all metadata including mtime (equivalent to fsync after each write) at higher cost

Data integrity completion can reduce the number of disk operations that are required for applications that don't need the guarantees of file integrity completion.

The incremental_async parameter is very much like incremental except the flushing is done asynchronously for higher performance. The data parameter tells the audit daemon to keep the data portion of the disk file sync'd at all times. The sync option tells the audit daemon to keep both the data and meta-data fully sync'd with every write to disk. The default value is incremental_async.

claim: POSIX rename() atomically replaces the destination file if it already exists, so no process ever observes newpath as missing during the operation
quote: If newpath already exists, it will be atomically replaced, so that there is no point at which another process attempting to access newpath will find it missing.

claim: rename() cannot cross mount points/filesystems on Linux; oldpath and newpath must be on the same mounted filesystem or it fails with EXDEV
quote: oldpath and newpath are not on the same mounted filesystem. (Linux permits a filesystem to be mounted at multiple points, but rename() does not work across different mount points, even if the same filesystem is mounted on both.)

claim: On NFS, rename() is not safe to assume failed just because it returned an error, because a server crash plus RPC retransmission can cause a spurious failure report for a rename that actually succeeded
quote: On NFS filesystems, you cannot assume that if the operation failed, the file was not renamed. If the server does the rename operation and then crashes, the retransmitted RPC causes a failure

claim: The write-new-file-then-rename technique is the standard userspace method applications use for atomic file updates on Linux, as opposed to in-place writes
quote: Either they use "weird user-space locking schemes", as databases typically do, or they write an entirely new file, then do an "atomic rename trick" to ensure the data is in place.

claim: Applications commonly misuse fsync() around the rename trick and end up losing data anyway, according to kernel filesystem developers
quote: Unfortunately, the applications often do not use fsync() correctly, so they lose their data anyway.

claim: fsync() does not guarantee the directory entry for the file has reached disk; a separate fsync() on a file descriptor for the parent directory is required for that
quote: Calling fsync() does not necessarily ensure that the entry in the directory containing the file has also reached disk. For that an explicit fsync() on a file descriptor for the directory is also needed.

claim: flock() locks are advisory only: a process with suitable permissions can simply ignore them and do I/O on the file anyway
quote: flock() places advisory locks only; given suitable permissions on a file, a process is free to ignore the use of flock() and perform I/O on the file.

claim: flock() over NFS was unsupported until Linux 2.6.12, when it began being emulated as fcntl byte-range locks over the whole file, meaning flock and fcntl locks interact with each other on NFS
quote: Since Linux 2.6.12, NFS clients support flock() locks by emulating them as fcntl(2) byte-range locks on the entire file. This means that fcntl(2) and flock() locks do interact with one another over NFS.

claim: flock() over SMB/CIFS was not propagated to remote clients at all until Linux 5.5, and after that point behaves as mandatory (not advisory) locking, unlike local flock semantics
quote: Since Linux 5.5, flock() locks are emulated with SMB byte-range locks on the entire file. ... Another important side-effect is that the locks are not advisory anymore: any IO on a locked file will always fail with EACCES when done from a separate file descriptor.

claim: write-file-atomic runs an fsync by default before the rename, and this can be disabled via an explicit option for performance
quote: If the **fsync** option is **false**, writeFile will skip the final fsync call.

claim: write-file-atomic serializes concurrent writes aimed at the same filename within one process into an in-memory queue, rather than letting them race
quote: If multiple writes are concurrently issued to the same file, the write operations are put into a queue and serialized in the order they were called, using Promises.

claim: As of Bun 1.3.14, the S3-to-file streaming form of Bun.write does not truncate a pre-existing larger destination file, leaving stale trailing bytes beyond the new content's length, even though other Bun.write forms (buffer source, file-to-file) do truncate correctly
quote: The first 4MB are overwritten but the file keeps its old length — the remaining 12MB of stale bytes survive. The FileSink used by the S3→file streaming path opens the destination without truncating it.

claim: The write-file-atomic npm package implements atomicity by writing to a uniquely-named temp file derived from the filename, pid and an invocation counter, then renaming it over the target on success, unlinking the temp file on any error
quote: The file is initially named filename + "." + murmurhex(__filename, process.pid, ++invocations).

claim: proper-lockfile uses the mkdir-based locking strategy specifically because mkdir is atomic across all filesystem types including network filesystems, unlike O_EXCL open
quote: This library utilizes the mkdir strategy which works atomically on any kind of file system, even network based ones.

claim: proper-lockfile's own documentation states that O_EXCL-based locking (used by the older isaacs/lockfile package) is broken on NFS filesystems and creates a race condition
quote: O_EXCL is broken on NFS file systems; programs which rely on it for performing locking tasks will contain a race condition.

claim: proper-lockfile detects a stale lock by periodically updating the lockfile's mtime while held, and checking that mtime against a stale threshold (default 10000ms, minimum 5000ms) to decide if a lock can be considered abandoned
quote: When a lock is successfully acquired, the lockfile's mtime (modified time) is periodically updated to prevent staleness. This allows to effectively check if a lock is stale by checking its mtime against a stale threshold.

claim: proper-lockfile explicitly does not protect against a lockfile being manually removed by an outside actor while it is supposedly held, and someone else then acquiring the lock right after
quote: A lockfile is manually removed and someone else acquires the lock right after

claim: proper-lockfile does not clean up its lock on a process killed with SIGKILL or a VM fatal crash such as out-of-memory, only on graceful exit
quote: proper-lockfile automatically removes locks if the process exits, except if the process is killed with SIGKILL or it crashes due to a VM fatal error (e.g.: out of memory).

claim: The 2009 ext4 zero-length-file data loss bug happened because ext4's delayed allocation meant a file replaced via truncate/O_TRUNC or rename-over-existing-file could end up with no data blocks allocated yet if the system crashed shortly after, unlike ext3's data=ordered mode which incidentally forced data out within its 5-second commit interval
quote: This solves the most annoying set of problems where an existing file gets rewritten, and thanks to the delayed allocation semantics, that existing file gets replaced with a zero-length file.

claim: On macOS, a plain fsync() call does not guarantee the drive has actually written data to the platter/media; Apple provides a separate F_FULLFSYNC fcntl specifically for applications like databases that need real write-ordering durability guarantees
quote: For applications requiring stricter data integrity guarantees, Mac OS X provides the F_FULLFSYNC fcntl option. This requests the drive to flush all buffered data to permanent storage with guaranteed write ordering. Databases and similar applications requiring strict write ordering should use F_FULLFSYNC.
quote_location: Apple fsync(2) man page mirror, DESCRIPTION

claim: Ted Ts'o (ext4 maintainer) states that applications worried about losing data on an unclean shutdown must call fsync themselves, because POSIX never guaranteed that a plain write would be durable within any particular time window, regardless of filesystem
quote: Long term, application writers who are worried about files getting lost on an unclean shutdown really should use fsync.

claim: On macOS, a plain fsync() call does not guarantee the drive has actually written data to the platter/media; Apple provides a separate F_FULLFSYNC fcntl specifically for applications like databases that need real write-ordering durability guarantees
quote: For applications requiring stricter data integrity guarantees, Mac OS X provides the F_FULLFSYNC fcntl option.
quote_location: Apple fsync(2) man page mirror, DESCRIPTION

claim: Even after a successful fsync(), the physical drive itself may still delay or reorder writing data to the actual storage media, so power loss can still leave only some or none of the data written
quote: while fsync() flushes data from the host to the drive, the drive itself may delay physically writing data to platters or write it out-of-order
quote_location: Apple fsync(2) man page mirror, DESCRIPTION

claim: SQLite's own documentation states that POSIX advisory locking is known to be buggy or unimplemented on many NFS implementations, including recent versions of Mac OS X, and recommends against putting SQLite database files on a network filesystem at all

claim: SQLite fsyncs the containing directory after creating its journal file on Unix specifically to push the new directory entry to disk, but this defense is incomplete because an unrelated concurrent filesystem operation in the same directory at the moment of a power failure could still cause the journal entry to be lost

claim: SQLite documents a real failure mode where a process renames the database file but forgets to also rename its associated journal file, leaving the journal orphaned and unable to be found on next open

claim: p-queue's onIdle() only resolves once queue.size===0 and queue.pending===0, i.e. all queued and running promises have completed, not merely that the queue is empty of waiting items.

claim: async-mutex explicitly documents that failing to call the release callback returned by acquire() will hold the mutex locked and will likely deadlock the application.

claim: mutexify guarantees strict FIFO fairness: the order in which the mutex was requested is the order in which access is granted.

claim: async-sema's Sema constructor supports an optional pauseFn specifically to apply backpressure upstream instead of letting waiting promises pile up and exhaust memory.

claim: Node's cluster module runs each worker as a fully separate OS process spawned via child_process.fork(), so an in-process mutex or lock object in one worker's memory has no effect on the others.

quote: When used with the default page size of 4096 bytes, this gives a maximum database size of about 17.5 terabytes. If the page size is increased to the maximum of 65536 bytes, then the database file can grow to be as large as about 281 terabytes.

claim: SQLite's theoretical max row count (2^64) is unreachable in practice because the 281TB max database size is hit first.
quote: The theoretical maximum number of rows in a table is 2^64 (18446744073709551616 or about 1.8e+19). This limit is unreachable since the maximum database size of 281 terabytes will be reached first.

claim: SQLite row size is bounded by SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH because the whole row is encoded as one BLOB during INSERT/SELECT.
quote: During part of SQLite's INSERT and SELECT processing, the complete content of each row in the database is encoded as a single BLOB. So the SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH parameter also determines the maximum number of bytes in a row.

claim: Practitioners on the official SQLite forum report that WAL mode is not faster than the default rollback journal for a heavy-insert (write-dominated) workload; WAL's advantage is concurrency, not raw single-writer insert speed.
quote: An heavy-insert scenario is not faster with WAL, in my experience.

claim: A physics-based ceiling exists for fsync-per-transaction throughput on rotating disks: about 60 transactions/sec absolute max for a 7200 RPM drive, versus roughly 10,000 TPS for a modern SSD and up to about a million TPS for a RAID array.
quote: 7200 RPM divided by 60 seconds per minute divided by 2 rotations per transaction yields 60 transactions per second, absolute max, hard-limited by physics, yet a lone modern SSD may achieve 10000 TPS, and a RAID of them may achieve a million TPS.

claim: A measured benchmark (stated hardware) found WAL mode reduces write throughput versus the default DELETE journal mode at low concurrency: -43% at 1 writer, -17% at 2 writers -- WAL only wins from 4+ concurrent writers onward.
quote: At 1 and 2 concurrent connections, writing to WAL reduces throughput by 43% and 17% respectively.

claim: In SQLite's own kvtest benchmark, writes were 5 to 15 times slower than reads on every tested system, for both direct file I/O and SQLite.
quote: Writes are slower. On all systems, using both direct I/O and SQLite, write performance is between 5 and 15 times slower than reads.

claim: Calling fsync() per file on direct-to-disk writes (the JSONL-style pattern) was measured at least 10x slower than SQLite's own single-file writes in SQLite's official benchmark.
quote: Invoking fsync() or FlushFileBuffers() per file causes direct-to-disk storage slowdown by factor of 10 or more versus SQLite writes.

claim: better-sqlite3 (a Node/Bun sqlite binding) measured, in WAL mode on a 2014 MacBook Pro, 62,554 individual-row inserts/sec.
quote: better-sqlite3 x 62,554 ops/sec ±7.33%

claim: better-sqlite3 measured 4,141 100-row-batched-transaction commits/sec in WAL mode (roughly 414K rows/sec when inserts are batched into single transactions).
quote: better-sqlite3 x 4,141 ops/sec ±4.57%
quote_location: Results, 2020-03-29, 'inserting 100 rows in a single transaction'

claim: HashiCorp Vault's audit subsystem is fail-closed: it guarantees every event reaches at least one enabled audit device, and documents that if all audit devices become unavailable Vault itself becomes unavailable.
quote: Vault sends the audit log entry of every API request and response to all enabled audit devices and guarantees that it saves to at least one of the enabled devices.

claim: Vault's file audit backend is described by its own vendor documentation as a deliberately minimal append-only file writer with no built-in rotation.
quote: This is a very simple audit device: it appends logs to a file.

claim: The JSON Lines specification recommends but does not require a trailing newline after the last record, and does not define any recovery procedure for a truncated/torn final line.
quote: Including a line terminator after the last JSON value in a file is strongly recommended but not required.

claim: SQLite's on-disk row overhead is small and structural: one varint for header length plus one serial-type varint per column, and both are usually a single byte each, with no fixed-width padding for TEXT/BLOB columns.
quote: The header size varint and serial type varints will usually consist of a single byte.

claim: Measured fsync latency scales enormously with storage hardware: a 7200 RPM HDD is limited to about 56 fsync-backed transactions/sec (~18ms each) with a single connection.
quote: A 7.2k RPM drive limits fully ACID transactions to ~56/second with single connection

claim: immudb's vendor documentation claims it 'can handle millions of transactions per second' for its hash-chained tamper-evident log, but states no benchmark hardware, dataset, or configuration for that number.
quote: Unlike blockchains, immudb can handle millions of transactions per second, and can be used both as a lightweight service or embedded in your application as a library.

claim: SQLite ATTACH DATABASE allows at most 10 attached databases by default; the hard maximum is 125 regardless of runtime tuning.
quote: The number of simultaneously attached databases is limited to SQLITE_MAX_ATTACHED which is set to 10 by default. The maximum number of attached databases cannot be increased above 125.
quote_location: Section 11, Maximum Number Of Attached Databases

claim: A monthly-partition-per-attached-file design in SQLite is limited by SQLITE_MAX_ATTACHED and rules out attach-based partitioning once partition count reaches the hundreds.
quote: The number of attached databases is capped by SQLITE_MAX_ATTACHED, which defaults to 10 and has a hard ceiling of 125. You can raise it up to that ceiling at runtime with sqlite3_limit(db, SQLITE_LIMIT_ATTACHED, n), but you cannot exceed 125. This rules out attach-based partitioning for anything with hundreds of partitions.

claim: Querying across SQLite time partitions is expressed as separate per-period tables combined by a UNION ALL view, which is read-only and does not prune non-matching branches automatically.
quote: Reads against events see everything. Writes have to target the correct underlying table, because a UNION ALL view is not writable on its own... The catch: SQLite does not prune the UNION ALL branches the way a partitioned planner would.
quote_location: Alternative 2: Separate tables plus a UNION ALL view

claim: A transaction spanning multiple ATTACHed SQLite databases is not guaranteed atomic when the main database runs in WAL mode.
quote: A transaction spanning multiple attached files is atomic only when the main database is in rollback-journal mode (or you enable the right settings); in WAL mode, atomic commits across attached databases are not guaranteed.

claim: logrotate's copytruncate option, needed when a process holds the log file open and cannot be told to reopen it, has a documented small window where log data can be lost between the copy and the truncate.
quote: Note that there is a very small time slice between copying the file and truncating it, so some logging data might be lost.

claim: logrotate supports both size-based and time-based (hourly/daily/weekly/monthly/yearly) rotation triggers, plus maxage to prune old rotated logs by age regardless of the rotate count.
quote: Log files are rotated only if they grow bigger than size bytes... Remove rotated logs older than <count> days. The age is only checked if the logfile is to be rotated.

claim: zstd at its fastest general setting achieves a 2.896x compression ratio on the Silesia corpus, beating zlib/gzip's 2.743x at similar or lower CPU cost, with far higher decompression throughput.
quote_location: Benchmark Results table (lzbench on Silesia corpus)

claim: zlib (the gzip algorithm) achieves a 2.743x compression ratio on the Silesia corpus at level -1, with roughly 5x lower compression throughput than zstd -1.
quote_location: Benchmark Results table (lzbench on Silesia corpus)

claim: SQLite VACUUM requires as much as twice the original database file size in free disk space while it runs, because it copies the database to a temporary file before overwriting the original.
quote: This means that when VACUUMing a database, as much as twice the size of the original database file is required in free disk space.

claim: Deleting rows in SQLite does not shrink the database file by default: freed pages are marked reusable but the file stays the same size unless VACUUM is run or auto_vacuum is enabled.
quote: Unless SQLite is running in "auto_vacuum=FULL" mode, when a large amount of data is deleted from the database file it leaves behind empty space, or "free" database pages. This means the database file might be larger than strictly necessary. Running VACUUM to rebuild the database reclaims this space and reduces the size of the database file.

claim: SQLite's auto_vacuum mode reclaims free pages automatically after deletes without a manual VACUUM, but at the documented cost of extra file fragmentation, and it does not compact partially filled pages the way VACUUM does.
quote: However, using auto_vacuum can lead to extra database file fragmentation. And auto_vacuum does not compact partially filled pages of the database as VACUUM does.

claim: PCI DSS's own documentation is echoed by secondary sources as requiring at least one year (12 months) of audit log history in total, with at least the most recent three months immediately available for analysis.
quote: In the case of PCI DSS, the audit history should be kept for at least one year and at least three months immediately available for analysis.

claim: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.15 (Logging) requires that logs recording activities, exceptions, faults and other relevant events be produced, stored, protected and analysed, without stating a numeric retention period.
quote: Logs that record activities, exceptions, faults and other relevant events should be produced, stored, protected and analysed.

claim: Because ISO 27001 leaves the retention duration to the organisation's own risk assessment, secondary guidance converges on 12 months as the de facto rule of thumb, with the most recent 3 months kept readily accessible.
quote: There is no single mandated period, but 12 months is the industry standard "rule of thumb" for retention, with the most recent 3 months being immediately available for analysis.
quote_location: FAQ: How long should we keep audit logs for ISO 27001?

claim: Neither the NIS2 Directive nor its Commission Implementing Regulation 2024/2690 (Section 3.2.5 of the Annex, covering log protection and retention) specifies a minimum log retention duration; it only requires logs be maintained, backed up and protected against unauthorised access and modification.
quote: CIR Section 3.2.5 does not specify a minimum retention duration. Neither does the NIS2 Directive itself.

claim: For NIS2 compliance in practice, a 12-month log retention split as 6 months hot (queryable) plus 6 months cold archive is cited as a defensible practical floor, with some member states' guidance citing an 18-month floor for essential entities.
quote: A 12-month minimum — 6 months in hot (online, queryable) storage plus 6 months in cold archive — is the practical floor that survives most national audits and supports forensic reconstruction across the widest range of incident scenarios.

claim: SOC 2's Trust Services Criteria do not prescribe an exact log/data retention duration; they require the organisation to define, document and enforce its own retention periods by data classification.
quote: While SOC 2 doesn't specify exact durations, it requires: Identifying and classifying sensitive data in databases, Defining retention periods by data type, Protecting data during retention, Ensuring secure and verifiable deletion afterward

claim: The GDPR's storage limitation principle (Article 5(1)(e)) requires personal data be kept identifiable for no longer than necessary for the purposes of processing, which bounds how long an audit log entry carrying personal data (e.g. a user ID performing an action) may be retained without a documented purpose.
quote: kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed

claim: SQLite multi-column indexes require an unbroken prefix of equality/IN-bound columns; the right-most usable column may carry the range/sort part, so a composite index for the per-user view should be (user_id, ts) with user_id first, not ts first.
quote: The initial columns of the index must be used with the = or IN or IS operators. The right-most column that is used can employ inequalities.

claim: SQLite supports DESC as a real physical index column order (schema format 4), not just query-time reversal; it has been understood since SQLite 3.3.0 (2006-01-11) and is the default schema format since 3.7.10 (2012-01-16).
quote: The descending index schema format (4) takes index sort order into account. Only versions of SQLite 3.3.0 (2006-01-11) and later are able to understand the descending index format.

claim: SQLite can satisfy ORDER BY rowid DESC (and by extension DESC on an indexed column) without a sort step by scanning the b-tree from the end backward instead of materializing and sorting the output.
quote: SQLite will still omit the sorting step. But in order for output to appear in the correct order, SQLite will do the table scan starting at the end and working toward the beginning

claim: A covering index (one containing every column a query needs) lets SQLite skip the second binary search into the base table, roughly doubling query speed for that lookup, marked in EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN as 'USING COVERING INDEX'.
quote: This saves one binary search for each row and can make many queries run twice as fast.

claim: In EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output, SCAN means SQLite iterates all rows of a table (even in index order), while SEARCH means only a subset of rows is visited; a 'USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY' line means the ORDER BY could not be satisfied by an index and a temporary sort structure was built instead.
quote: "SCAN" is used for a full-table scan, including cases where SQLite iterates through all records in a table in an order defined by an index. "SEARCH" indicates that only a subset of the table rows are visited.
quote_location: eqp.html section 1.1 Table and Index Scans

claim: When a temp b-tree is needed for sorting, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN emits a literal 'USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY' node, and this can be eliminated by adding an index on the ORDER BY column(s).
quote: In this case using the temporary b-tree can be avoided by creating an index

claim: A partial index (CREATE INDEX ... WHERE ...) covers only the subset of rows matching its WHERE clause, which the SQLite docs state directly improves both query and write performance because the index is smaller and only needs updating for the exceptional rows it covers.
quote: When used judiciously, partial indexes can result in smaller database files and improvements in both query and write performance.

claim: SQLite's partial-index usability test is a documented, deliberately incomplete syntactic match (not a real theorem prover): a query WHERE-term must textually match an OR-term in the index's WHERE clause, or be a comparison on a column the index restricts with 'IS NOT NULL' -- otherwise the optimizer will not use the partial index even if it is logically implied.
quote: SQLite does not have a sophisticated theorem prover with which to determine W⇒X. Instead, SQLite uses two simple rules to find the common cases where W⇒X is true, and it assumes all the other cases are false.
quote_location: partialindex.html section 3 Queries Using Partial Indexes

claim: ANALYZE statistics (sqlite_stat1) are a one-time snapshot the query planner loads at schema-read time; they are not updated as the database changes, so a growing audit table needs periodic re-ANALYZE (documented as PRAGMA optimize) to keep query plans good.
quote: Statistics gathered by ANALYZE are not updated as the content of the database changes. If the content of the database changes significantly, or if the database schema changes, then one should consider rerunning the ANALYZE command in order to update the statistics.

claim: The offset method must count-and-discard all rows from the start of the result up to the requested page, so the scanned index range (and thus cost) grows with page depth; the seek/keyset method instead re-enters the index directly at the last-seen key via a WHERE predicate, so it does not re-scan prior pages.
quote: Nevertheless, the database must count all rows from the beginning until it reaches the requested page.
quote_location: use-the-index-luke.com Paging Through Results, offset method section

claim: A qualitative (hardware/row-count unspecified) benchmark chart in Use The Index, Luke shows the seek method holding roughly constant response time across pages 0-100 while the offset method's response time grows visibly from about page 20 onward -- indicative but not a rigorous measured number.
quote: The accuracy of measurement is insufficient to see the difference on the left hand side of the chart, however the difference is clearly visible from about page 20 onwards.

claim: When the sort key is not unique, keyset pagination needs a tiebreaker column (e.g. a primary key) appended both to the index and to the ORDER BY / WHERE predicate as a row-value comparison, because paging fundamentally requires a deterministic row sequence and ORDER BY on a non-unique column alone does not guarantee one.
quote: Paging requires a deterministic sort order.
quote_location: use-the-index-luke.com Paging Through Results, Important box

claim: The keyset/seek predicate for a (ts, rowid) tiebreaker pairing is the row-value comparison WHERE (ts, rowid) < (?, ?) ORDER BY ts DESC, rowid DESC, built on a composite index CREATE INDEX ... ON sales(sale_date, sale_id) that carries the same column order as the ORDER BY.
quote: CREATE INDEX sl_dtid ON sales (sale_date, sale_id)
quote_location: use-the-index-luke.com Paging Through Results, deterministic order-by example

claim: SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN documents that a compound query (UNION, UNION ALL, EXCEPT, INTERSECT) is planned per-branch, and when the branches must be merged into one order, SQLite either builds a temporary b-tree over the union ('UNION USING TEMP B-TREE') or runs each branch as an order-preserving co-routine and does a sorted MERGE -- either way a distinct, documented merge step is inserted whenever a chronological query spans more than one source.
quote: The "USING TEMP B-TREE" clause in the above output indicates that a temporary b-tree structure is used to implement the UNION of the results of the two sub-selects. An alternative method of computing a compound is to run each subquery as a co-routine, arrange for their outputs to appear in sorted order, and merge the results together.

claim: SQLite imposes no arbitrary limit on the number of indexes a table may carry (only a per-index column-count limit via SQLITE_LIMIT_COLUMN); the documentation gives no numeric guidance on how many indexes an append-heavy table can 'afford' before writes suffer -- that tradeoff is left to the general principle that every index adds write cost, not a stated threshold.
quote: There are no arbitrary limits on the number of indices that can be attached to a single table.
